name: wasm-tools
desc: Low level tooling for WebAssembly in Rust
why: Swiss-army knife for WebAssembly binaries, letting you dissect, validate and convert the format by hand.

brief.what_it_is: wasm-tools is a Bytecode Alliance command-line program and set of Rust libraries for working with WebAssembly modules and components at a low level. The single wasm-tools binary has subcommands that take a .wasm binary or a .wat text file as input. They validate it, print it as text, parse text back to binary, mutate or generate test modules, strip or demangle sections, dump binary structure, and build or inspect components and WIT interface files. Output goes to stdout or to a file with -o.
brief.why_it_exists: The README describes the project as 'CLI and Rust libraries for low-level manipulation of WebAssembly modules,' and says the CLI 'contains useful tools for debugging WebAssembly modules and components.' It also states that the repository 'strives to implement any standardized proposal to WebAssembly.'
brief.how_it_works: Each CLI subcommand wraps a library in the same repo, such as wasmparser for validate, wat for parse, wasmprinter for print, wasm-smith for smith, and wasm-mutate for mutate. Commands follow shared conventions: stdin is read when no file is given, output goes to stdout unless -o is passed, -t emits text format, and -v adds log verbosity. Commands can be piped together. Proposal support is switched by a --features flag, and stage 4+ proposals are on by default in validation.

commands_seen.context: Builds and installs the CLI from source using Cargo. Requires a Rust toolchain.
Installs the precompiled release artifacts with cargo-binstall instead of building from source.
Validates a binary WebAssembly file. A .wat file is also accepted and converted to binary first.
Validates with a default-enabled proposal (simd) turned off.
Converts a binary module to WebAssembly text format and writes it to foo.wat.
Converts a text-format module to binary.
Produces a mutated module with a fixed seed and pipes it into validate to check that the output is still valid.

commands_seen.cmd: wasm-tools demangle foo.wasm | wasm-tools strip | wasm-tools objdump
commands_seen.context: Demangles Rust and C++ names in the name section, strips other custom sections, then lists the remaining binary sections.
Prints the WIT interface of a component.
Wraps a core wasm module as a component. The core module must already have WIT metadata embedded.

brief.install_notes: Precompiled artifacts are published on the GitHub releases page for each release. Building from source needs the Rust toolchain, installed from rust-lang.org, and uses cargo install --locked. cargo binstall can fetch the precompiled binaries instead. No accounts, hardware, or runtime setup are mentioned. Converting a WASI core module into a component needs an adapter file passed with --adapt, such as wasi_snapshot_preview1.reactor.wasm, which the user has to supply.
brief.standout: It is a single binary that covers reading, writing, validating, and fuzzing WebAssembly. It includes wasm-smith (generates valid modules from a seed), wasm-mutate, and wasm-shrink for test-case work. Its subcommands pipe into one another, and its proposal list is shown with the stage status of each feature.
brief.status: Maintained. The README describes a release workflow run from GitHub Actions, a patch-release process for older 1.N.0 lines, and an active list of proposals. The README gives no release date or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the releases or commits pages, so the exact date of the latest release is unknown. It also states that releases have no strict cadence and are made as needed.
brief.caveats: The C/C++ bindings in crates/c-api do not cover all of the functionality. Only the wasm-tools CLI and the wat crate are considered API-stable. The other crates are versioned 0.X.Y and may break on each release, so the README says to expect upgrade friction. The README says to prefer the libraries over the CLI when embedding. wasm-tools compose is marked deprecated. The project is triple licensed under Apache 2.0, Apache 2.0 with LLVM exceptions, and MIT. Proposals beyond stage 4 are off by default in validation and may change.
